title: Pan-Seared Ribeye with Red Wine Pan Sauce
short: A steakhouse crust, butter-basted finish and a glossy two-minute pan sauce.
keywords: Pan-Seared Ribeye with Red Wine Pan Sauce, date night, dinner for two, classic, fancy
intro: This is the dinner that turns a home kitchen into a steakhouse for the night. A properly dry, properly salted ribeye hits a ripping-hot pan, gets basted with butter, garlic and thyme, then rests while the pan gives you a glossy red wine sauce from the browned bits left behind. Nothing here is difficult. It rewards attention, not skill.
why: Sizzle, aroma and a sauce made in front of your guest. Slicing and fanning the steak at the table looks professional and takes ten seconds.

video.title: How to cook the perfect steak

ings.i: ribeye steaks, about 300 g (10 oz) each and 3–4 cm (1¼–1½ in) thick
unsalted butter, divided (2 tbsp + 1 tbsp cold)

ings.h: 120 ml (½ cup)
ings.i: dry red wine (Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot)

ings.h: 120 ml (½ cup)

steps.t: Season the steaks on all sides with the kosher salt at least 45 minutes before cooking (or up to 24 hours ahead, uncovered on a rack in the fridge). Leave them at room temperature for the last 30–45 minutes and pat completely dry with paper towels.
Heat a heavy 30 cm (12 in) cast-iron or stainless skillet over high heat for 3–4 minutes, until a drop of water skitters and evaporates instantly. Add the oil and swirl.

Lay the steaks in the pan, away from you. Sear without moving for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms, flip and sear 2 minutes more. Hold each steak on its edge with tongs for 30 seconds to render the fat cap.

Turn the heat to medium-low. Add 2 tbsp butter, the garlic and thyme. Tilt the pan and spoon the foaming butter over the steaks continuously for 1–2 minutes. Pull them at 52°C (125°F) on an instant-read thermometer for medium-rare.
Move the steaks to a board or rack, grind over pepper and rest for 8 minutes. The temperature will climb about 3°C (5°F) while they rest.

Make the sauce: pour off all but 1 tbsp fat. Over medium heat, cook the shallot for 1 minute. Add the wine and scrape up the browned bits; reduce by half, 2–3 minutes. Add the stock and reduce until syrupy and about 80 ml (⅓ cup) remains, 3–4 minutes.
Off the heat, whisk in the mustard, the cold 1 tbsp butter and any juices from the resting steaks. Taste and adjust the salt.
Slice the steak against the grain into 1 cm strips, fan onto warm plates, spoon the sauce beside it and finish with flaky salt.

tips: A dry surface is the whole secret to a crust. If the steak is wet, it steams before it browns.
If your pan is smaller than 30 cm, cook one steak at a time and keep the first warm on a rack in a 95°C (200°F) oven.
Open a window or switch on the hood before the oil goes in. Smoke alarms are not romantic.
makeahead: Salt the steaks the night before and mince the shallot in the afternoon. Everything else happens in the last 20 minutes.
plating: Warm the plates in a low oven. Fan the slices in a slight curve, pool the sauce next to the meat rather than over the crust, and add a small tangle of watercress for color.
wine: Cabernet Sauvignon or Argentine Malbec: the tannin cuts through the marbling.
zero: Sparkling tart-cherry juice with a bruised rosemary sprig.

faq.q: Can I use a different cut?
faq.a: Yes. New York strip and sirloin work with the same method. Lean cuts like filet cook faster, so start checking the temperature a minute earlier.
It is the single best $15 you can spend for cooking to impress. Touch tests are unreliable, especially when you are nervous.
